diagrams.caption: Equal threats, so Black runs out first: Black 5 is elsewhere, and White 6 connects the ko. Black 7 puts White's four stones in atari, White 8 is elsewhere, and Black 9 captures them, but White 10 takes the vital point of the pyramid four: dead.
One threat more for Black. Black 5 retakes after a threat elsewhere, White has no threat left and plays elsewhere with White 6, and Black 7 captures the stone at B18: eyes at A19 and B18.

Black 5 ataris White's stone at D19, but it is no threat: White 6 connects the ko. Black 7 captures the stone, but the eye at D19 is false because of White's stone at E18: White 8 makes Black 9 fill it. Black stays dead.

text: White 4 in Diagram 1 has just captured Black 1, so Black cannot retake at once and must find the first threat. With equal threats Black runs out first, and White 6 in Diagram 2 connects and kills. With one threat more than White, Black retakes and lives (Diagram 3). That is KO−. The solver's ko tables agree: an equal count fails, one more succeeds.

The site's tutorial counts a ko White took first as KO+ only when Black has a local threat that White lacks. Black has none: White answers Black 7 or Black 9 of Diagram 2, played as a threat, by connecting the ko, and Black dies the same way. Black 5 in Diagram 4 ataris a stone, but White can ignore it, and D17 and D16 only fill Black's own liberties. After Black's retake in Diagram 3, every White move except a retake lets Black live, so White has no local threat either: a plain direct ko.

Both reviewers confirm KO−. S[KO+] looks like a slip: it is what besogo's editor writes for a ko unless the author presses the '-' button. The author's comment on this leaf, 'this is NOT the Ko to aim for', also fits a ko that is bad for Black.
